**Page:** First T. Rex Fossil Found in Golden – https://weare.mines.edu/?sid=840&gid=1&pgid=8727&cid=17996&ecid=17996&crid=0&calpgid=8505&calcid=17322  
**Evidence**  
- “Did you know the first ever T. rex fossil was found right here in Golden 150 years ago, the same year Mines was founded? In 1874, a Jarvis Hall student discovered a fossilized tooth while hiking on South Table Mountain with his professor, geologist **Arthur Lakes**.”  
- “The tooth was initially misidentified as coming from a sauropod, and it wasn't until **2000** that it was identified as that of a **Tyrannosaurus rex**, making it the first ever fossil discovered from that species.”  
- “**Lakes** became a professor at Mines in **1880** and excavated many sites across Colorado during the **‘dinosaur bone rush’**,….”

**Coverage**  
- **Entities:** Arthur Lakes (geologist, professor); Jarvis Hall student (unnamed); South Table Mountain (location).  
- **Dates:** 1874 (discovery of tooth), 1880 (Lakes becomes professor), 2000 (identification as T. rex).  
- **Conditions:** Tooth misidentified as sauropod until 2000; first ever T. rex fossil found in Golden 150 years ago (≈1974‑present).  
The list includes all distinct facts that the supplied page explicitly states; it is a complete set of the page’s relevant information.

**Missing**  
- Study published December 2011 on rocks, minerals, history, and ancient life of a specific place.  
- Census report for a year after 2010 but before 2024 that was questioned.  
- Petition filed challenging census discrepancies.  
- Details of dinosaur bone discovery in 2000 and subsequent confirmation by two individuals (one collaborated on a 2001 reconstruction, the other earned Ph.D. in 1974).  
- Any other biographical or research details beyond Arthur Lakes’ role and the T. rex tooth discovery.

**Next links**  
- https://www.mines.edu/museumofearthscience/  – may contain catalog and research details about geologic sites studied by Lakes.  
- https://www.goldenhistory.org/  – could hold historical context about Golden’s paleontological sites, including the 1874 discovery.

### Page note: https://iowageologicalsurvey.uiowa.edu/dinosaurs-iowa
Reader state: complete; relevance: partial
**Page:** Dinosaurs in Iowa | Iowa Geological Survey - College of Engineering | The University of Iowa  
URL: https://iowageologicalsurvey.uiowa.edu/dinosaurs-iowa  

**Evidence**  
- “Charlie Gillette of Dickinson County picked up a dark‑colored, 3‑inch fossil bone from a load of landscaping gravel that came from a nearby gravel pit.”  
- “His uncle Jack Neuzil, a retired educator and dinosaur enthusiast, saw the bone and suspected that it could be a dinosaur vertebra.”  
- “The discovery of Iowa’s first identifiable dinosaur bone was soon reported in the _Des Moines Register_ (9/7/2000).”  
- “The fossil is a tail vertebra from an unknown dinosaur, possibly a hadrosaur.”  
- “Following this discovery, a second dinosaur vertebra from Iowa has come to light thanks to Doris Michaelson of Bellevue.”  
- “Her father, John Holdefer, had a keen eye and was fascinated by the rocks and fossils that he saw as a Materials Inspector for the Iowa Highway Commission.”  
- “Sometime in the mid‑1930s he picked up a fossil bone from a conveyor in a gravel pit near Akron in Plymouth County.”  
- “The bone was kept on a shelf and occasionally used as a doorstop in the family’s home.”  
- “It is a partially weathered 4‑inch dinosaur vertebra, likely from a hadrosaur.”  
- “Learn about dinosaurs in Iowa in _Iowa Geology_, No. 26, 2001, p. 4‑9.”

**Coverage**  
- **Entities:** Charlie Gillette, Jack Neuzil, Doris Michaelson, John Holdefer, Iowa Geological Survey.  
- **Dates/Years/Measurements:** 3‑inch fossil bone, 9/7/2000 (report date), 4‑inch dinosaur vertebra, mid‑1930s (bone discovery time), 2001 (publication _Iowa Geology_ No. 26).  
- **Conditions/Units:** 3‑inch, 4‑inch bone measurements; “tail vertebra,” “partially weathered,” “wild dinosaur.”  
- **Scope:** Iowa fossil discoveries; Iowa Geological Survey involvement.  
- The list is **complete** for the facts present on this page; no tables or truncated lists appear.

**Missing**  
- No evidence of animal footprints.  
- No mention of a 2011 study on rocks/minerals/history/ancient life of a particular place.  
- No details about a census report, petition, 2000 bone discovery by the subject, or collaborators in dinosaur reconstruction.  

**Next links**  
1. https://iowageologicalsurvey.uiowa.edu/igs/publications/uploads/2015-03-07_08-03-12_ig-26.pdf – could provide the “Iowa Geology, No. 26, 2001” publication that may contain more about the 2000 bone.  
2. https://iowageologicalsurvey.uiowa.edu/igs/publications – general publications index; may lead to 2011 study.  
3. https://iowageologicalsurvey.uiowa.edu/about-us – could give information about Iowa Geological Survey staff, possibly related to the subject.
